Audio Version:
📷Listen now · 24:17

By: Dr.s Jill Glasspool Malone and Robert W. Malone

“In fourteen hundred ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue.”
In the 1960s, when I was a child in elementary school, California was enjoying its golden years. Agriculture was thriving, vast cattle ranches still dotted the arid landscape, and the aerospace industry was reaching extraordinary heights. Hollywood was the undisputed capital of American moviemaking, and the state’s population and economy were growing by leaps and bounds. Brand new, uncrowded freeways made it easy to get around. California represented the best and brightest of America, a place of opportunity, innovation, ambition, and seemingly limitless possibilities. People from around the world looked to California as a symbol of what America could accomplish. There was a palpable sense of optimism about the future, a belief that hard work, ingenuity, and determination could make almost anything possible.

I grew up in Goleta, on California’s Central Coast, where Spanish heritage was woven into the landscape, the architecture, the place names, and the history we learned in school. We studied the Spanish missions, the California vaqueros, the great ranchos, and the Chumash Indians who had inhabited the region long before Europeans arrived. We learned about the hardships and injustices experienced by the Chumash, but we also learned about the explorers, missionaries, ranchers, and settlers who shaped California. I remember reading Richard Henry Dana Jr.’s Two Years Before the Mast, with its vivid descriptions of life aboard a sailing ship and the California coast in the 1830s. These stories brought our local history to life. They gave us an appreciation for the people who came before us, the hardships they endured, and the extraordinary changes that had transformed California into the place we called home.
And, of course, we learned American history. We learned about Christopher Columbus and his three small ships, the Niña, the Pinta, and the Santa María, sailing across the vast Atlantic in 1492. We learned about Spain’s role in the voyages of discovery, the European settlement of the Americas, the thirteen colonies, the American Revolution, and the founding of the United States. These stories were taught with a sense of wonder and pride. We were encouraged to admire the courage of explorers, the determination of pioneers, and the extraordinary accomplishments of the men and women who helped build this nation. We learned that America was a land of opportunity, a country founded on the ideals of liberty and self-government, and a place where ordinary people could aspire to extraordinary things.
That education gave us something important. It gave us a connection to our history, a sense of belonging, and pride in the country we had inherited. It taught us that America was worth appreciating, worth defending, and worth improving. It gave us patriotism, not as a political slogan or an obligation imposed from above, but as something that grew naturally from learning about the people, events, sacrifices, and achievements that had made our country possible.

The Columbus I learned about in elementary school was a navigator who crossed an immense ocean in three small wooden ships, undertaking a voyage whose outcome was anything but certain. We memorized the familiar rhyme, learned the names of the ships, and imagined what it must have been like to sail westward into waters that few Europeans had ever crossed. We were also taught about the people who already inhabited the Americas, the Spanish missions, and the hardships and injustices of colonization. We were instructed to read “Ishi in two worlds,” the heartrending story of one of the last remaining Native Californians to grow up outside the surrounding Anglo-Spanish-American culture. Learning about those darker chapters did not prevent us from appreciating the extraordinary accomplishments that had shaped the world we inherited.

Today, the educational emphasis is quite different. The Pulitzer Center distributes classroom materials that explicitly seek to reframe American history around 1619 and the institution of slavery.

Launched by The New York Times in 2019, the 1619 Project seeks to reframe American history around the arrival of enslaved Africans in colonial Virginia rather than the founding of the United States in 1776. Its central premise is that slavery and its legacy are fundamental to understanding virtually every aspect of American society. What began as a magazine publication has grown into a substantial educational enterprise, supported by the Pulitzer Center, with more than 100 curricular resources, a national network of more than 400 educators across 30 states, professional-development conferences, and classroom materials extending from elementary school through law school. Its original educational guides reportedly received more than one million accesses during their first five years.

The American Federation of Teachers (AFT), led by Randi Weingarten, has actively promoted the project through its Share My Lesson platform and partnered with the Pulitzer Center to distribute teaching resources. This is no longer simply a controversial interpretation of American history. It is an organized effort to influence how American history is taught, supported by educational institutions, philanthropic funding, and a major national teachers’ union. The concern is not that children are learning about slavery, which is an essential part of American history, but that a contested interpretation placing racial oppression at the center of America’s origins is being promoted as a foundational framework for understanding the country and its institutions.

The Pulitzer Center identifies Meta, Open Society Foundations, Rockefeller Brothers Fund, and several other philanthropic organizations among supporters of its 1619 education initiative

California’s own Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum directs attention toward colonialism, systemic oppression, and social transformation. Educational organizations publish elementary-school lessons encouraging children to reconsider the celebration of Columbus. These are not imaginary controversies invented by political commentators. The materials are publicly available, and their authors openly describe the changes in historical interpretation they seek to promote.

There is an important difference between teaching children that Columbus and America’s founders were imperfect men, sometimes responsible for grave injustices, and teaching American history through an interpretive framework in which exploitation and oppression occupy the center of the national story. The first expands historical understanding. The second raises legitimate questions about how the nation’s achievements, founding ideals, and historical failures are weighed against one another. What children learn to admire, what they learn to condemn, and what they learn to regard as their national inheritance will influence how they understand the country in which they live.

And what are the results of this re-educational programming?

📷

The generational divide is striking. According to Gallup’s analysis of surveys conducted between 2021 and 2025, only 41 percent of Generation Z adults described themselves as extremely or very proud to be American, compared with 75 percent of Baby Boomers and 83 percent of the Silent Generation. These numbers raise an important question about the relationship between what children are taught and how they eventually regard their country. For generations, American schools emphasized the nation’s founding ideals, its achievements, and the responsibilities of citizenship, alongside its historical failures. American schools taught Americanism, a belief in the greatness of America.

The change extends beyond national pride. A September 2020 Pew Research Center survey found that 86 percent of Black adults believed America had not done enough to secure racial equality, up from 78 percent just a year earlier. Nearly two-thirds reported recently educating themselves about the history of racial inequality.

In 2020, 86% of black and Hispanic adults said that the country hasn’t done enough to address racial inequality.

📷

These findings emerged during a period of intense national conflict over race and reflect a growing emphasis on racial identity and historical injustice. They also raise a question worth examining: whether educational approaches that increasingly organize American history around racial divisions help students understand and overcome those divisions, or risk reinforcing them.

Today, most educational programs place considerably greater emphasis on systemic oppression, racial injustice, and the shortcomings of American institutions. There is no question that the shift has contributed to the growing generational divide in national pride.

The generational divide is unmistakable. Gallup found that only 41 percent of Generation Z adults are extremely or very proud to be American, compared with 75 percent of Baby Boomers. YouGov polling also shows that younger Americans are far more likely to view Christopher Columbus unfavorably than their grandparents. These surveys reveal a profound shift in how younger generations regard their country and its historical figures. When schools change the way American history is taught, it is reasonable to ask whether they are also changing how children understand what it means to be American.

Children begin forming attitudes about race, identity, and belonging long before they are capable of critically evaluating complicated historical arguments. Developmental research shows that racial attitudes emerge in early childhood and are shaped by the messages children receive from adults, peers, and institutions. This places an enormous responsibility on schools. Teaching any child to judge classmates through inherited categories of racial guilt or victimhood will reinforce the very prejudices education should help overcome.

When Racial Justice Became an Industry

The death of George Floyd in May 2020 ignited a wave of anger that swept across the United States. The demonstrations, riots, destruction of property, and demands for institutional change did not emerge in an organizational vacuum. Long before Floyd’s death, major philanthropic foundations had been financing an extensive network of racial-justice organizations, activist training programs, and political advocacy groups. The Ford Foundation helped establish the Black-Led Movement Fund in 2016, while George Soros’s Open Society Foundations contributed to the network through the Borealis Philanthropy.

The money supported grassroots organizing, direct-action training, leadership development, and campaigns to transform public institutions. Following Floyd’s death, the funding expanded dramatically. In July 2020, Open Society announced $220 million in commitments to Black-led organizations and racial-justice initiatives. What began as public outrage over a death in police custody rapidly became a nationwide political and institutional movement backed by substantial financial resources.

The nationwide protests and riots following George Floyd’s death in 2020 came at an enormous human and economic cost. According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), at least 25 people were killed in demonstrations and incidents connected to the broader political unrest. The Major Cities Chiefs Association documented more than 2,000 police officers injured between May and July, while the total number of civilian injuries remains unknown.

Rioting, arson, vandalism, and looting spread across more than 140 American cities. According to the Insurance Information Institute, the destruction resulted in more than $2 billion in insured losses, making the unrest the costliest civil disorder event in American insurance history. The violence accompanying the movement left communities devastated, businesses destroyed, and a financial burden extending well beyond the insured losses.

The infrastructure for mobilizing protests, amplifying political messages, and pressing institutions for change had been built over years. Organized advocacy and spontaneous public anger reinforced one another. The result was a period in which race became an organizing principle for political debate, corporate policy, university administration, and educational “reform.”
The timing coincided with a troubling change in racial attitudes. In the American National Election Studies data, the average favorability rating that Black Americans ages 18–29 gave white Americans fell from approximately 64 in 2016 to 47 in 2020, before partially recovering to 56 in 2024. The pattern documents that the extraordinary emphasis and money spent on amplifying racial division during 2020 had the desired effect: it reinforced racial tension.

The relationship between the protest movement and education is especially relevant. The 1619 Project had launched in 2019, before Floyd’s death, and was already promoting an interpretation of American history centered on slavery being the foremost catalyst for the founding of America, with continuing consequences that last until now.

There is an intellectual connection worth examining as well. Marxist and neo-Marxist traditions have long emphasized the relationship between social institutions, power, economic inequality, and political change.

The educational philosophy known as critical pedagogy was heavily influenced by Paulo Freire, a Brazilian socialist educator whose work drew extensively on Marxist theories of oppression and class struggle. Freire believed schools should do more than teach facts and practical skills. Education should encourage students to question established institutions, identify perceived systems of oppression, and become agents of social and political change. His ideas have become influential in American universities and schools of education and helped shape approaches to teaching that emphasize social justice and political consciousness. Basically, these ideas have woven Marxist theories into educational curricula

The events of 2020 therefore deserve examination not only as a protest movement but as a turning point in institutional approaches to race and Marxist theory. The documented funding networks, rapid expansion of racial-justice programs, and contemporaneous deterioration in some measures of interracial attitudes are related. The resulting institutional changes have deepened the divisions they sought to address.

From Columbus to the Classroom

The controversy over Christopher Columbus is no longer simply about a fifteenth-century explorer. It is part of a much larger struggle over how American history is interpreted and transmitted to the next generation. Consider how differently children can encounter the same historical figure. One lesson introduces Columbus through navigation, maritime exploration, the dangers of the Atlantic crossing, and the extraordinary consequences of 1492.

Another begins by asking students to reconsider whether Columbus deserves to be celebrated or even remembered, emphasizing conquest, enslavement, and the experiences of Indigenous peoples. Both subjects belong in a serious history curriculum, but the choice of emphasis matters, particularly for young children who are still developing their understanding of history, identity, and national belonging.

The movement to reshape historical education is neither imaginary nor confined to individual classrooms. The Pulitzer Center’s 1619 Project Education Network has offered grants to educators developing curricula centered on slavery, racial inequality, and their contemporary consequences. Its supporters have included George Soros’s Open Society Foundations, alongside Meta and other major philanthropic organizations. The initiative has also reached university schools of education, where future teachers are trained. Its published grant objectives go beyond historical instruction to include preparing students to participate in social change.

The more immediate concern is whether students are learning to understand the constitutional republic, including its remarkable achievements, or being encouraged to view its institutions primarily through the lens of historical oppression.

The American founders understood the dangers of concentrated political power and unchecked majority rule. They established a representative republic with divided powers, constitutional limitations, and protections for individual liberty. These institutions were imperfectly applied from the beginning, but they also provided mechanisms through which later generations fought to abolish slavery, expand citizenship, and secure civil rights. Students deserve to understand that history alongside the injustices that made those struggles necessary. The enduring question is whether contemporary historical education gives them the knowledge to evaluate and preserve their constitutional inheritance, or teaches them to regard that inheritance chiefly as a problem to be overcome.
From Education to Ideological Transformation

The influence of critical theory and Marxist-inspired approaches to education extends well beyond elementary and secondary schools. American universities now offer degrees, certificates, and professional training in diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), social justice, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles.

At Penn State, a Social Justice certificate examines how unequal power relationships shape society. Northwestern University teaches students to analyze intersectionality and develop approaches to social change. More explicitly, the University of Massachusetts Amherst offers graduate courses titled Liberatory Pedagogies for Social Transformation and Confronting Oppression in Education. These are not fringe pamphlets circulating among student radicals. They are formal academic programs, including programs designed to train future educators.

Author James Lindsay, in The Marxification of Education (2022), traces these developments to the influence of Marxist and neo-Marxist thinkers, particularly the above-mentioned Brazilian Marxist and educator Paulo Freire. Lindsay argues that critical pedagogy transforms education from the transmission of knowledge into a means of developing political consciousness and promoting institutional change. These types of university programs explicitly describe social transformation as an educational objective.

text:
Wes, the problem with your argument is neatly encapsulated in your assertion that your premise “will always be confirmed because it cannot be otherwise”.

You’ve constructed a premise that you declare incapable of falsification, then treat individual examples as confirmation of its universal truth. That’s circular reasoning, not logical necessity.

And there’s an obvious difficulty with your argument in the very Tennessee case you’re citing.

The defence expressly offered to respect Lee’s female identity and use she/her pronouns while also presenting evidence of her biological sex. The two were plainly not considered mutually exclusive.

The error identified by the appellate court was the exclusion of relevant evidence, not the recognition of Lee’s gender identity. You’re conflating those two things and extrapolating from one erroneous judicial ruling to the supposed inevitable corruption of every institution that recognises transgender people.

And now you’re attempting to draw a symmetry between a completed criminal trial, examined on appeal, and early newspaper coverage of an entirely separate incident.

In Tennessee, we have a judicial ruling found erroneous on appeal, resulting in a retrial.

In Chicago, we have a newspaper reporting criminal allegations and quoting an activist’s interpretation of the circumstances. That interpretation has no judicial authority whatsoever.

You could read the same incident reported in two different newspapers and find markedly different emphases, quotations and narratives. We see that routinely in the UK. That’s editorial selection, not evidence of judicial corruption.

You may reasonably criticise the Tribune’s editorial choices, but how does that establish your proposition that transgender recognition necessarily corrupts institutional standards?

You claim an ocean of evidence, yet you’re selecting examples from fundamentally different contexts and declaring both confirmation of a conclusion you’ve already decided must be true.

That’s not logical necessity. It’s confirmation bias.

PERKINS: When the State Tries to Train the Church https://t.co/lsuuDnlW6H
If voters are trying to imagine what the nation would look like under the socialist policies of a Democratic majority in Congress, look no farther than California.

Governor Gavin Newsom (D) and the Democratic supermajority in both chambers of the state legislature offer an extensive list of policies flowing from the same socialist and Marxist ideology being championed by the ascendant wing of the Democratic Party.

The latest example is AB 1803, signed by Governor Newsom last week. Authored by Assemblyman Josh Lowenthal (D), the law requires employers with five or more employees to add training on hate speech to the growing list of California’s harassment-training laws.

Lowenthal said, “California must make meaningful progress to train Californians on the danger of hate speech not only in the workplaces, but in society as a whole.”

The law describes speech covered by the training as speech that “vilifies, humiliates, or incites hatred” against people based on protected characteristics.

And what are those protected characteristics? They include religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, and reproductive health decision-making — which includes abortion.

There are others, but those are enough to raise serious questions for Christians and religious organizations.

First, there is no clear legal definition of hate speech. Whatever the intent, the effect is to give the term enormous elasticity. Who decides when a deeply held religious conviction crosses the line from disagreement into “humiliation” or “vilification” and is then defined as hate speech?

Second, California law does not make sufficiently clear how this new mandate applies to churches and religious ministries. That ambiguity itself should concern anyone who values religious freedom, because the protected categories include subjects on which biblical Christianity makes unmistakable moral and theological claims.

Jesus said in Matthew 19 that the Creator “made them male and female,” and then described marriage in terms of a man and a woman. Does teaching those words humiliate someone who rejects the biblical understanding of sex and marriage?

What about Jesus’s words in John 14: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me”? Christianity is inherently exclusive in its truth claims. Could that someday be deemed vilifying toward another religion?

This is why California’s law should concern the church and everyone else, for that matter. When state officials declare the state needs to train society on what is appropriate speech, all of society is in trouble. Frankly, the state of California should not be instructing the church — the church should be instructing the government on what is right and wrong.

For Christians, this is an Acts 4 moment. When Peter and John were ordered not to speak or teach in Jesus’s name, they answered: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you more than to God, you judge.”

California is not merely a laboratory for the Left; it is a warning to the rest of America. The question for voters is whether California’s experiment stops at the state line, or comes to Washington. And the question for the church is even more fundamental: when government demands that we compromise biblical truth, will we have the courage of Peter and John to stand firm and speak it?

text:
Lightweight prospect Bobby Scanlon (pictured) goes to 30-0-1 with a 10-round unanimous decision over Gale Kerwin at Madison Square Garden on July 18, 1958.

From boxrec on Bobby Scanlon, 42-12-1 with 12 KO wins, active from 1954-66:

Bobby Scanlon had a very difficult childhood growing up in Father Baker's orphanage. Possessing choirboy looks, Scanlon was frequently the target of tougher kids. Scanlon turned to boxing and became the orphanage champion. He began his pro career in mid 1954. During the first three-and-a-half years of his career, he was undefeated in 32 fights, at 31-0-1. He competed mainly in New York City, with occasional stops in Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Erie, Pennsylvania.
His sister, Carol, remembers her brother driving his powder-blue Thunderbird around the First Ward. He is also remembered as a very generous brother who returned home during the Christmas season to buy gifts for his sisters.
Bobby Scanlon's manager, Mike Scanlon (no relation), then moved Bobby and his other three fighters--Rocky Fumerelle, Richie Todaro and Joey Giambra--to San Francisco in 1957. After a brief stay Todaro returned to Buffalo. The remaining three fighters occupied the same house along with Mike Scanlon, and they all became top contenders in their divisions. Scanlon improved his winning streak to 32 in California. He defeated such top fighters as Lauro Salas, Wallace (Bud) Smith, Joey Lopes and Dave Gallardo.
Following the March 1957 fight with Davy Gallardo, Scanlon broke with his manager Mike Scanlon. Bobby was already showing a dislike for the tough training techniques utilized by Mike. His contract was purchased by Art Benjamin, and later by Nick Kobseff and Lou Sabella. Fred Apostoli, former middleweight champion, would later become Bobby Scanlon's trainer.
According to Rocky Fumerelle, "Bobby Scanlon was his own worst enemy." Scanlon was good-looking and a good fighter. He was very popular among the Irish of San Francisco. If he would have remained in better shape and maintained a regular training schedule, "I have little doubt that Bobby Scanlon would have been the Lightweight champion of the world."
From late 1958 to early 1960 Scanlon not only saw his winning streak come to an end, but he also lost five of seven fights. Scanlon's winning streak came to an end when he suffered a third-round knockout to Paolo Rosi. Prior to this fight Scanlon was rated third in the Lightweight Division behind Rosi and Carlos Ortiz. Soon after his initial loss to Rosi, Scanlon lost another ten-round decision to Paolo. Scanlon also lost a pair of ten-round decisions to Johnny Gonsalves, as well as a decision to Al Urbina. But Scanlon did win a big ten-round decision over Orlando Zulueta.
Scanlon then returned to Buffalo to fight fellow Buffalonian Jackie Donnelly. In a hard-fought 12-round fight, Scanlon won the New York State Lightweight championship. It was one of Scanlon's biggest paydays, as he collected $4,937 for the fight.
Following the first Johnny Gonsalves fight, Scanlon began to suffer double vision. It got worse as he prepared for the second fight with Gonsalves. The problem continued through the Jackie Donnelly fight, as well as an August fight with Francisco Santos. Scanlon laid off from boxing for a year before he returned to fighting again in 1962. Things were not the same. In addition to the double vision, Scanlon had suffered a serious kidney and liver infection. He changed managers four times, and saw his level of competition go down, losing seven of his last thirteen fights.
Although Scanlon was fighting less frequently in 1965 and 1966, he was still experiencing eye problems. He retired from boxing in mid-1966. After he retired from the ring everything went downhill. Early in his boxing career Scanlon had been offered a job in public relations with the Oakland Raiders football team, but now there were few job offers. Although he became deeply religious, his physical and mental health began to deteriorate. Scanlon was struggling to adjust to life without boxing, struggling to restore some meaning to his life, when he died in a fire at the Hotel Lackawanna on June 23, 1975. He was only 39 years old. His final record was 42-12-1.

Stats Show That Lesbianism May Be a Fad... But Was it Ever Really ‘In’? 📷📷📷📷📷October 11, 2026📷Quinn DelamaterNewsAt the age of 14, every teenager experiences a rite of passage: the start of high school, The desire to conform infiltrates vulnerable minds, leading some to question their identity. For the last decade, “conformity” in many high schools across looked like identifying or allying with the LGBT community. But now, experts aren’t so https://t.co/hP2mJNauBr 2021, 30% of girls in their freshman year of high school identified as lesbian or bisexual. But in 2025, that number dropped to 17%, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported. Jean Twenge, a professor of psychology at San Diego State University, wrote in her Substack “Generation Tech” last month, “Much of the change in LGB identification among girls is a drop in identifying as bisexual. … Once again, the 9th graders show the largest change. While 26% of 9th grade girls identified as bisexual in 2021, only 13% — half as many — did in 2025.”“It really does look like a free fall,” Twenge added. “But what’s causing it is unclear.”Senior scholar at UCLA Jody Herman told The Washington Post, “The study doesn’t provide confidence intervals to determine whether the differences are actually significant. The narrative around a decline in LGBT identity among youth has been around for a while now. We’ll continue to look at trends over time in our work, but the evidence provided so far for a decline leaves more questions than answers.”According to Twenge’s analysis of the 2025 CDC data, the same does not go for young men. “The decline appears to be driven almost entirely by girls. Identifying as LGB dropped from 27% in 2023 to 22% in 2025 among girls, and from 9% to 7% among boys,” she continued. “The previous increase in identifying as LGB was also larger among girls, with a 128% increase (more than doubling) from 2015 to 2021 among girls and a 99% increase (doubling) from 2015 to 2023 among boys.”Her analysis continued, “For 12th graders, 17 and 18 years old, identifying as LGB declines only a few percentage points between 2023 and 2025 (from 18% to 16%). There’s more of a decline for 11th graders (16 and 17 years old) and more still for 10th graders (15 and 16 years old) ... But the headline result is for 9th graders (14 and 15 years old): Identifying as LGB absolutely plummets between 2023 and 2025, from 17% to 11%.”The statistics generated varying reactions on social media, as people offered their own rationale for the shift. One X user commented on the statistics, “If bigotry was the issue, we’d see declines in all groups . The likely answer is that girls this age are notoriously prone to social contagions and following the crowd. For the incoming freshmen class, the fad has run its course.”Another user wondered if the decreasing number is the result of cultural whiplash to the progressive agenda: “[It] went too far, specifically the trans movement. The gender madness, the integration of men into women’s sports etc. it all went too far and a backlash is forming.” A third user agreed, “Since the change happened in such a short period of time, we know it's not biological evolution or genetics. Clearly, it's cultural.”Joseph Backholm, host of the “Politics for Happy People” podcast told The Washington Stand that he believes that the 2021 statistics are the result of a social contagion. “Sexual desires and identity are complicated topics, but this is very strong evidence that Gen Z wasn't really born that way,” he explained. “It was fashionable to have an LGBTQ+ identity, and it seems to now be less fashionable.”

Bedjine’s career belongs in this conversation

Bedjine offers a useful example of a younger woman establishing an artistic presence through recordings, collaboration and live-event billing. Her work alongside K-Dilak is a professional partnership, not a reason to disregard her contribution. Sharing a project with a man does not make a woman’s voice, interpretation or audience relationship less her own.

The duo’s recorded work predates 12 ERA’s Boston concert by years. Apple Music lists “Pouki’n Te Marye,” featuring Bedjine, in 2020 and “Engra,” featuring Bedjine, in 2021. It credits both K-Dilak and Bedjine as artists on the 16-track album Misyon Akonpli, released October 11, 2024. Those credits document sustained musical work rather than a career that exists only through commentary about gender.

Assessing Bedjine’s talent remains an artistic judgment. What the record establishes is that she has an identifiable body of work and a billed role in a joint act. A fair evaluation listens to her performances and examines her contribution instead of treating collaboration as evidence of dependence.

M2 Miami’s official event archive lists “Bedjine Kdilak Album Release Party in Miami” for Saturday, November 30, 2024, in Miami Beach, with doors at 10 p.m. That corroborates the advertised event and date described by the contributor. It establishes that Bedjine was billed in a substantial professional venue well before the October 2026 MGM occasion. The listing alone does not establish the number of attendees, tickets sold or the exact performance format.

M2 describes its venue as 35,000 square feet with customizable configurations, dedicated lighting and sound systems, and private VIP spaces. That description supports treating it as a serious event setting. Square footage, however, is not a crowd count, and the M2 event should not be assigned an attendance figure that its records do not supply.

The comparison has an important limit: a joint album-release event is not the same category as a concert headlined by a solo artist. If Carel meant the first solo female-led concert meeting a particular capacity threshold in Boston, he should specify that category and substantiate it. A narrower claim cannot simply be assumed after a sweeping statement circulates.
Celebrate the Achievement, Check the History: Bedjine, 12 ERA and Carel Pedre’s Reported “First Big Concert” Claim

text:
You correctly note that international protection applicants in Direct Provision receive only the Daily Expenses Allowance and cannot claim Jobseeker’s Allowance or Child Benefit until status is granted, that Stamp 2 students are generally excluded, and that employer-tied Stamp 1 holders have limited access. Those restrictions exist. https://t.co/DrukTCje93 https://t.co/tQA2CJ6qC1

The claim that this prevents the outcome described in the prior post is incomplete. Once refugee or subsidiary protection status is granted, the recipient is entitled to the same social welfare benefits as Irish citizens, subject to the Habitual Residence Condition, which is satisfied upon grant. That includes Child Benefit (€140 per child per month) and means-tested Jobseeker’s Allowance (€254 per week for an adult over 25, plus qualified adult and child supplements). Households of five children can therefore reach the €700 Child Benefit plus adult support totals previously calculated. https://t.co/aLFEdwSdOf https://t.co/npxnJ1Tf8y

Grant volumes are not the 0.7 percent of population figure offered. Parliamentary data show refugee status and subsidiary protection grants totaling more than 20,000 across 2015–early 2026, with several thousand per year in recent cycles (for example, over 3,700 first-instance positive decisions in 2025 alone, plus appeals). Applications have run in the tens of thousands annually in peak years. Once granted, those individuals and their qualifying family members enter the ordinary welfare system. https://t.co/js4JxXLuY1 https://t.co/WebN5dJvdz

The prior post’s ESRI analysis of CSO SILC data and the Carol Nolan parliamentary figures on Jobseeker’s Allowance recipients remain the record: non-Irish nationals are over-represented relative to population share in long-term unemployment payments, and family payments are higher for certain origin groups because of larger average household size under universal Child Benefit plus means-tested adult support. Native Irish households of identical size and means receive the same rates. The disparity is produced by the combination of continued inflows, status grants, higher fertility, and rules that treat habitual residents equally once the status threshold is crossed. https://t.co/v834b8RH0j https://t.co/OgvP0Ggw7F

The least-cost complete correction is to publish the status-grant volumes, the post-grant eligibility rules, and the household-size arithmetic side by side with the existing restrictions for applicants. Voters and the Oireachtas already have the statutory levers: tighter Habitual Residence Condition application, status-based waiting periods before full means-tested access, or reforms to universal Child Benefit that account for household structure. No new apparatus is required beyond the published rates, grant statistics, and the data already cited.

text:
I recently received a direct message on X from a young Northern Irish lady who asked me the following:

"Sir Timothy, you have often spoken of your Ulster birth, your attachment to the Protestant faith, and your devotion to the traditional teachings of the Church of England. May I ask, therefore, why you have never joined the Orange Order? Is it because of its political associations, its reputation for sectarianism, or the suggestion that it has Masonic connections? Surely, for a man of your convictions, the Order's defence of Protestantism ought to make it a natural home. Or do you have reservations about the Order itself?"

In all honesty, it is a perfectly fair question, and one which deserves a more considered answer than the raising of an eyebrow, the adjustment of one's cuffs, and the customary observation that life is already burdened with more societies than any sensible man can reasonably attend.

I was born in Carrickfergus, in the north of Ireland, and I have never felt any inclination to conceal the fact. Ulster is not merely a geographical expression in my private history; it is a part of my inheritance, with all the memories, loyalties, affections, and historical complexities that such an inheritance entails. One does not cease to belong to the place of one's birth merely because one has travelled, acquired books, developed opinions, or discovered that the world is considerably larger than the map upon which one first learned to locate it.

Nor have I ever been ashamed of being a Protestant. Indeed, I have always regarded the English Reformation as a matter of considerable theological and historical importance, and I remain attached to the old formularies of the Church of England: the Book of Common Prayer, the Thirty-Nine Articles, and the Ordinal. I have a particular affection for the language of the Prayer Book, which possesses the rare quality of being both beautifully fashioned and theologically serious without feeling obliged to advertise either accomplishment.

One might reasonably suppose, therefore, that I should have found a natural home in the Orange Order. I understand the historical circumstances in which it arose, the importance which its members attach to the Protestant inheritance, and the place it has occupied in the social and political life of Ulster. I do not regard these matters as trifling, nor would I presume to dismiss the convictions of those who have devoted themselves to the Institution.

Nevertheless, I have never joined it.

The explanation is neither particularly mysterious nor, I hope, offensive. I have simply never considered membership necessary to the expression of my religious convictions. I am an Anglican because I believe in the faith as I have received and understood it, not because I require an additional institutional allegiance to certify the fact. My Protestantism is a matter of conscience; my Anglicanism is a matter of ecclesiastical identity; and my Ulster birth is a fact of geography and biography. These three things may coexist perfectly well without requiring me to enrol in every organisation with which one or another of them has historically been associated.

There is, moreover, a distinction which I have always considered worth preserving: the distinction between defending a religious tradition and identifying oneself with every organisation that undertakes to defend it.

The two activities are not necessarily incompatible, but neither are they identical. A man may defend the authority of Scripture, uphold the doctrines of the Reformation, cherish the Prayer Book, and remain faithful to the historic Church without becoming a member of a Protestant fraternity. Equally, a man may join such a fraternity from sincere conviction without thereby becoming a more faithful Christian than his neighbour who declines to do so.

I have never been persuaded that the sincerity of one's faith can be measured by the number of associations whose membership certificates one is able to display.

My reservations, insofar as I have any, concern the broader question of religious identity and communal allegiance. Ulster's history is not a simple tale, and it would be a discourtesy to its people to pretend otherwise. Its religious divisions have been shaped by centuries of political conflict, competing national aspirations, genuine theological disagreements, inherited grievances, and loyalties which have sometimes outlived the circumstances that originally gave rise to them.

I have no intention of resolving that history in a paragraph, still less of pretending that one can understand it by distributing praise and blame with the impartiality of a clerk balancing his ledger. But I do believe that the Christian must exercise a certain vigilance whenever religious conviction becomes inseparable from political identity.

The danger is not that a Christian should care about the history of his people. On the contrary, gratitude for one's inheritance is a perfectly respectable virtue. The danger arises when the defence of that inheritance begins to be treated as a sufficient definition of one's Christian duty, or when loyalty to a community is permitted to determine in advance the moral standing of everyone outside it.

The Gospel makes demands upon us which are not always convenient to our inherited sympathies. It commands us to love our neighbours, to forgive our enemies, and to examine our own conduct with at least as much seriousness as we examine the conduct of those with whom we disagree. These obligations are not suspended at the border of a political tradition, nor do they become less binding when the people on the other side of a religious divide have behaved badly.

This does not mean that theological differences are unimportant. I should be the last person to suggest that all doctrines are interchangeable, that the differences between Anglicanism and Roman Catholicism are imaginary, or that historical controversies can be settled by declaring everyone equally right. Such a conclusion would be intellectually lazy and theologically incoherent. Christian charity does not require the abandonment of conviction; it requires that conviction be exercised without malice.

I can disagree with a Roman Catholic about the authority of the Pope, the nature of the Church, or the interpretation of Scripture without regarding him as an enemy by definition. I can defend the Thirty-Nine Articles without supposing that every person who rejects them must therefore be personally unworthy of my respect. There is, after all, a difference between believing a proposition to be false and believing the person who holds it to be beyond the reach of Christian charity.

It is a difference which our age, despite its prodigious production of moral declarations, has not always found easy to maintain.

The question of Freemasonry introduces another consideration. The Orange Order is not simply a branch of Freemasonry, nor should the two institutions be treated as though they were interchangeable. There are, however, historical similarities in their fraternal organisation, terminology, ceremonial forms, and use of lodges. Historians have discussed the influence of Masonic models upon aspects of early Orange organisation, although similarity and historical influence do not establish institutional identity.

I would therefore be reluctant to repeat the assertion, sometimes made rather confidently, that the Orange Order is itself a Masonic organisation. That would require a more precise argument than the observation that both institutions have lodges, ceremonies, and distinctive forms of regalia.

Nor would I wish to make an accusation merely because it suited an argument I had already decided to win. The pursuit of truth is not improved by exaggeration, even when the exaggeration happens to be directed at an institution of which one is suspicious.

Nevertheless, I have my own reservations about certain forms of fraternal obligation and ritual, and I would want to understand their nature before committing myself to them. As an Anglican, I am conscious that questions concerning oaths, religious language, and the obligations assumed by members of a society can have theological significance. Whether a particular practice is acceptable must be considered on its own merits; it cannot be settled merely by attaching the word Masonic to it, as though that adjective were a complete theological argument.

I do not, therefore, claim that the Orange Order is unacceptable to every Christian, nor do I presume to judge the conscience of every man who joins it. I can only say that I have never found sufficient reason to enter it myself.

My religious allegiance is already substantial enough. The Church of England has provided me with a liturgy, a calendar, a body of doctrine, and a long inheritance of prayer and worship. It has given me words with which to confess my sins, to intercede for others, to commemorate the dead, and to approach the mysteries of the Christian faith. I have never felt that this inheritance was deficient merely because it did not require me to join an additional fraternity.

If anything, I have sometimes suspected that the modern appetite for multiplying affiliations arises from a certain anxiety about belonging. We seem increasingly determined to establish who we are by identifying the societies, causes, parties, movements, and communities to which we belong. We assemble our identities as though we were compiling a philatelic album, carefully filling each empty space with the appropriate emblem.

But a human soul is not a collection of membership badges.

I have spent a considerable portion of my life studying words, symbols, and the histories of things which other people have sometimes dismissed as insignificant. Stamps, runes, old books, ecclesiastical formularies, and the curious survivals of ancient custom have all taught me something about the manner in which human beings preserve their past. They have also taught me that a symbol may acquire meanings beyond those originally intended, and that an institution may come to represent something rather different to different generations of its members.

It is therefore possible to respect the historical significance of the Orange Order without regarding membership as a religious obligation. It is possible to understand why a man might join it without supposing that every Protestant ought to follow him. And it is possible to remain attached to Ulster without allowing one's birthplace to prescribe the whole course of one's conscience.

I should add, lest my position be misunderstood, that I have no desire to cultivate an artificial neutrality. I am not ashamed of my convictions, and I have no wish to dissolve the particularities of my inheritance into some vague and fashionable sentiment in which every historical distinction is regarded as an inconvenience. I believe that the Christian faith makes definite claims upon the intellect and the conscience. I believe that traditions deserve to be understood before they are discarded, and that the past should not be judged solely by the moral vocabulary of the present.

But I also believe that loyalty is most honourable when it remains voluntary, and that conviction is most credible when it does not require constant public demonstration.

Perhaps this is where my answer finally rests. I have never felt that I needed to prove my Protestantism by joining the Orange Order, any more than I need to prove my affection for cricket by joining every cricket club in the British Isles. One may love the game, understand its traditions, defend its peculiar virtues, and still decline the invitation to sit on another committee.

The comparison is not entirely frivolous. Cricket has taught me that the rules of a game are important precisely because they permit a contest to take place without requiring the participants to hate one another. There are occasions when tempers rise, when an appeal is disputed, and when a batsman departs with a degree of reluctance which suggests that he has mistaken the pavilion for a court of final appeal. Yet the game survives because its principles are larger than the immediate passions of those who play it.

Religious and political life are, of course, more serious matters than cricket. But I sometimes wonder whether we might profit from remembering that a disagreement need not become a declaration of enmity, and that loyalty to one's own side does not require the denial of every virtue in another.

So, if you ask whether I am an Ulsterman, I shall answer in the affirmative. If you ask whether I am a Protestant, I shall answer without hesitation. If you ask whether I am an Anglican of the old persuasion, I shall probably begin discussing the Prayer Book before you have finished your tea.

But if you ask whether I am an Orangeman, I must disappoint you.

I am not.

I remain, instead, a man who wishes to preserve his religious inheritance without confusing it with every political or fraternal expression that has grown up around it; a man who would rather examine an institution carefully than condemn it carelessly; and a man who believes that his neighbour's conscience is not his property to regulate.

There are enough divisions in the world without my manufacturing additional ones for the sake of a more easily understood biography.

And if, after all this, you still consider me insufficiently straightforward, I can offer you one final consolation. My personal motto has never been PROUD TO BE UNAMBIGUOUS.

It is, as you may know, PROUD TO BE CONFUSED.

I have found the distinction surprisingly useful.

I’d like to go back to a simpler time…

⬇️⬇️⬇️⬇️⬇️

I liked it when a man was a man. 

I liked it when a woman was a woman. 

I liked it when women’s rights weren’t being trampled on by men pretending to be women. 

I liked it when people knew what a woman was. 

I liked it when kids were allowed to be kids. 

I liked it when tomboys were allowed to be girls. 

I liked it when children weren’t being lied to, manipulated, put on puberty blockers, sterilized, mutilated and sentenced to life long medicalization by the gender cult. 

I liked it when child abusers weren’t considered heroes. 

I liked it when the LGB community wasn’t chained to the alphabet mafia. 

I liked it when future generations weren’t being burdened with insurmountable debt. 

I liked it when families weren’t being taxed into a state poverty and then offered rebates - paid for by other families who are on the verge of being taxed into a state of poverty. 

I liked it when you could buy groceries and go out for dinner on the same day. 

I liked it when food-banks weren’t overwhelmed. 

I liked it when there weren’t homeless people everywhere. 

I liked it when there weren’t tent cities in every major city. 

I liked it when there weren’t people suffering from drug addiction and unaddressed mental illness lining the streets. 

I liked it when I wasn’t the only white person in the room.

I liked it when immigration was sustainable. 

I liked it when immigrants came to this country for a better life that they were willing to work for - and not just handouts.   

I liked it when people weren’t chanting “Death to Canada” in the streets. 

I liked it when they weren’t burning the Canadian flag. 

I liked it when people weren’t being pushed into oncoming traffic for carrying the Alberta flag. 

I liked it when Canadians weren’t booing the American National Anthem because orange man bad. 

I liked it when the federal government wasn’t freezing bank accounts and laughing about it. 

I liked it when people didn’t die waiting in line for “free healthcare.”

It was a simpler time. 
It was more enjoyable.
People weren’t so angry. 

Does that make me racist? Transphobic? A bigot? A traitor? Ignorant? White trash? Far right?

Yeah, sure - I guess it does. 

And that’s fine with me. 

Because I liked it better back then.

text:
Russia's crypto rails just went live — and they're state-owned 🎄

The Central Bank of Russia added Sberbank ($SBER) to its authorized digital-asset exchange register, letting the country's largest lender offer crypto products to retail and corporate clients under new federal law. Sberbank says structured products will roll out by December 1 — a concrete date inside a regulated framework, not a pilot.

Same morning, Bank PSB-backed A7 unveils A7 International: a USDT-to-SWIFT settlement service for foreign trade operators and individuals.

The pitch: convert USDT into fiat across borders at ~0.3% — against typical remittance fees of 3%–30%. Launch date: today, 13 October.

Why Asia traders should care:
• Moscow is wiring stablecoins into SWIFT-compatible corridors while Western rails stay fragmented
• Two state-controlled banks now sit on both ends — on/off-ramps and cross-border settlement
• Compliance and KYC requirements keep it inside Russia's regulated perimeter, not a shadow-rails setup
• For APAC desks looking at ruble-settled trade or CIS-linked counterparties, the plumbing is finally legible

The bigger frame: Russia's regime has shifted from blanket anti-crypto posture to a federal-law, bank-mediated model — a third path between the US enforcement-first stance and Hong Kong's licensing-first approach. Sberbank's December timeline is the test of whether a state-bank-led retail crypto market can actually scale outside the offshore era.

Meanwhile the macro backdrop for this week's Asia open is loud: BTC pivoting near $82K with the Fear & Greed Index cooling to 56 (neutral, down from extreme greed in late August), DXY pressing an 18-month high near 102.56, and U.S. CPI on deck before the Fed's October meeting. Risk appetite isn't gone — it's just thinned out.

For traders waking up in Singapore, Hong Kong and Seoul: the Russia-crypto story is no longer a headline about sanctions — it's a regulated, bank-issued product launch with a dated rollout and a settlement rail going live today. Watch how Sberbank structures its first retail offerings and how A7's 0.3% fee holds up against actual flows.

NFA — do your own research on counterparty exposure before sizing any Russia-linked position.

text:
No other human being comes close to this!

Tell me, what false prophet would stand in prayer as an obligation for six hours almost every night, then perform many more prayers during the day ON TOP of the five daily prayers? These were prayers that only he was obligated to perform by God. We are not expected to do them because we don’t have the ability to, as Allah gave him the strength to do so. What false prophet would continuously fast outside the month of Ramadan, going many days without breaking his fast? What kind of man would do this if he wanted convenience, power, and wealth? What human being had the ability, stamina, and strength to do all this besides a prophet of God?

He would feed 70 people a day, twice a day. All the while, he was teaching and lecturing on Islam and the Quran, providing guidance and counseling on marriage and social issues, issuing rulings as a judge and governor of a state, and serving as an arbiter. He was essentially a psychological and spiritual counselor, arguably the greatest military commander and warrior in history, a husband, a father, and a nephew. He married older women who were widows of war and had children, helping protect them from financial and housing insecurity, while also strengthening tribal alliances by marrying women from different tribes as a political strategy. What human being in history do you know who had the wisdom, genius, stamina, strength, patience, and tolerance to do all these things, day and night? No human being could do all this without direct help, guidance, and strength from God!

The tribes of Makkah offered him money, power, wealth, women, and status in exchange for stopping his preaching of Islam. He told them that even if they placed the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left, he would never stop, by Allah! What false prophet, grifter, or conman behaves like this? He turned down power, wealth, money, women, and status. This completely undermines the claim that he was a false prophet, grifter, or conman because it makes no sense to think someone seeking those things would behave this way.

Prophet Muhammad died without leaving behind money or wealth for his family to inherit. He was a Messenger of God, and no special privileges were to be given to his family. That’s why none of his sons survived: they all died in infancy or childhood, preventing any direct male successor to him. That’s also why he never named any of his cousins, such as Ali, or his nephews, Hasan or Husayn, as his successor. In Islam, lineage plays no role in religious authority, and he didn’t want to give anyone the impression that his family had special rights or privileges. There are many examples of this throughout his life, when he could have treated his family differently in matters of rulings and justice, but he didn’t.

His mother and father died before he was eight years old. He lost his beloved first wife, Khadijah, along with his grandfather and uncle, within a relatively short period. He lost nearly all his children during his lifetime; all but one died before him, and that daughter died a few months after him. His life was marked by pain and tragedy, as were the lives of the other prophets of God!

Allah gave him the choice to be a prophet-king like Solomon, but he chose the life of a poor and simple prophet to identify with the poor and needy. text:
This is why he’s the greatest man and history and no other human being comes close to this’

Tell me, what false prophet would stand in prayer as an obligation for six hours almost every night, then perform many more prayers during the day ON TOP of the five daily prayers? These were prayers that only he was obligated to perform by God. We are not expected to do them because we don’t have the ability to, as Allah gave him the strength to do so. What false prophet would continuously fast outside the month of Ramadan, going many days without breaking his fast? What kind of man would do this if he wanted convenience, power, and wealth? What human being had the ability, stamina, and strength to do all this besides a prophet of God?

He would feed 70 people a day, twice a day. All the while, he was teaching and lecturing on Islam and the Quran, providing guidance and counseling on marriage and social issues, issuing rulings as a judge and governor of a state, and serving as an arbiter. He was essentially a psychological and spiritual counselor, arguably the greatest military commander and warrior in history, a husband, a father, and a nephew. He married older women who were widows of war and had children, helping protect them from financial and housing insecurity, while also strengthening tribal alliances by marrying women from different tribes as a political strategy. What human being in history do you know who had the wisdom, genius, stamina, strength, patience, and tolerance to do all these things, day and night? No human being could do all this without direct help, guidance, and strength from God!

The tribes of Makkah offered him money, power, wealth, women, and status in exchange for stopping his preaching of Islam. He told them that even if they placed the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left, he would never stop, by Allah! What false prophet, grifter, or conman behaves like this? He turned down power, wealth, money, women, and status. This completely undermines the claim that he was a false prophet, grifter, or conman because it makes no sense to think someone seeking those things would behave this way.

Prophet Muhammad died without leaving behind money or wealth for his family to inherit. He was a Messenger of God, and no special privileges were to be given to his family. That’s why none of his sons survived: they all died in infancy or childhood, preventing any direct male successor to him. That’s also why he never named any of his cousins, such as Ali, or his nephews, Hasan or Husayn, as his successor. In Islam, lineage plays no role in religious authority, and he didn’t want to give anyone the impression that his family had special rights or privileges. There are many examples of this throughout his life, when he could have treated his family differently in matters of rulings and justice, but he didn’t.

His mother and father died before he was eight years old. He lost his beloved first wife, Khadijah, along with his grandfather and uncle, within a relatively short period. He lost nearly all his children during his lifetime; all but one died before him, and that daughter died a few months after him. His life was marked by pain and tragedy, as were the lives of the other prophets of God!

Allah gave him the choice to be a prophet-king like Solomon, but he chose the life of a poor and simple prophet to identify with the poor and needy. What human being do you know in history who was this humble? He used to sit on the floor, blending in with his companions. text:
Only those people with a passion for knowledge, whilst remaining impartial enough that they can entertain ideas without necessarily accepting them. Will come anywhere close to be named educated. And being on the right path if they endeavor towards wisdom. People like these will also be the kind that can offer up arguments for their case, without parroting established authorities on subjects. Hitler was a man like that. He was an intellectual who despised intellectuals. It seems curious and perhaps something of a paradox at first. But once you understand what it means to be a state loyalist intellectual. Or someone who reads with a purpose only to abuse knowledge by pulling the wool over peoples eyes. You understand why he despised the intellectual class. And we suffer from many of these types of people every day. We have a record breaking number of intellectual shills running around everywhere making all sorts of claims, that for the unprepared and uneducated becomes truth. 

The older one becomes, and the more one looks around. One realizes how the uneducated people, seems to be living in parallel lives to how i described the educated people. Rather than the pursuit of knowledge and truth, to better our people. The interests of our uneducated people have spiraled out of control into becoming either interests in the carnal. Or confused and self-deceiving activism that - despite their well intentioned effort, really only acts completely contrary to the interest of their own kind. People commit national suicide without being aware of it. 

The want for gold, makes it necessary to prevent a population from becoming too conscious, and thereby more open to plunder.  Rather than pursuing knowledge. Our people have found themselves put into a position - where they let knowledge come to them through others (intellectuals) or through the press (mass media) or through which ever leader and administration happens to preside at the moment. And these sources are hardly ever questioned, for in the minds of people. The thought apparently never occurs to them that, what they are told are either flawed, half-truths or a politically motivated narrative to fit an obvious course. One which people are not meant to understand, and even less to question.   

To resist people or institutions who are established enough to be called an authority on a subject.  It requires a resilient cognitive mind, and a disciplined critical thinking rather than passive reliance on external sources. It is the reactionary minds that dismisses things offhand. And often if not entirely - it is through emotion than logic that it happens. And people are highly emotional and much less reasonable i find in lack of any true knowledge. 

Though the responsibility of education lies primarily on oneself, in order to understand the world properly. The real holocaust, is what happens to our children who are led and guided through the worst institutions we have devised in our modern societies. The schools. I fear that the only thing that is living inside the majority is demoralization. Because we have never seen this kind of self-flagellation and despising of ones own nation and heritage as we are witnessing on display before our very eyes each day.   

I recall reading through Herodotus once, and found a quote that stuck with me ever since.   

"the greatest pain a man can experience, is to have insight into much; and power over nothing"

“Let me make this shit perfectly clear.

I know Florida has never elected a Black governor, and yes, the election of Byron Donalds would be historic. As a Black Floridian, I understand the significance of seeing someone who looks like me occupy the Governor’s Mansion. But history alone will NOT get my vote.

This isn’t about Byron Donalds being Black, and it isn’t simply because he’s a Republican. It’s no secret that I’m a moderate Democrat, and have crossed party lines before when I believed the Republican candidate was the better person to lead the great state of Florida.

But, child please! It will be a cold day in hell before I cast my vote for Byron Donalds, and here’s why.

Representation means absolutely nothing to me if the person representing us lacks the integrity, independence, courage, and conviction to stand up when it matters!  Time and time again Byron has demonstrated he’s no independent critical thinker. 

Black sisters and brothaz, Byron Donalds is no Barack Obama. He is no General Colin Powell. And I refuse to become so mesmerized by the possibility of Florida electing its first Black governor that I ignore the man’s record, his alliances, his rhetoric, and what I believe his leadership would mean for Florida. I am TIRED of symbolism being offered as a substitute for substance.

After years of watching DeSantis policies coming out of Tallahassee that I firmly believe have chipped away at civil rights protections, attacked diversity initiatives, and diminished how Black history is taught and discussed, I cannot vote for someone simply because his skin looks like mine. So yes, David Jolly is a white man. I am not voting for a complexion. I am voting for leadership. I am voting for policies. I am voting for character. I am voting based on who I believe will respect the history and civil rights of ALL Floridians rather than continue tearing away at them.

My vote come November 2026, will be for David Jolly (FULL STOP)! Florida deserves better than another four years of division, political bullshit, and culture wars. I love this state far too much to vote based on skin color.

The Steele dossier, which underpinned much of the early coverage and FISA warrants, was later revealed to contain significant unverified or false claims.
2. Scaramucci–Russian investment fund story (2017)
CNN published a story claiming the Senate Intelligence Committee was investigating a meeting between Anthony Scaramucci and the head of a Russian investment fund. The network fully retracted it the next day, stating it “did not meet CNN’s editorial standards,” and apologized. Three journalists, including a senior editor, resigned.
3. Hunter Biden laptop as “Russian disinformation”
CNN (along with other outlets) amplified or treated as credible the claim by 51 former intelligence officials that the New York Post’s reporting on the laptop had “all the classic earmarks of a Russian information operation.” The laptop and its contents were later authenticated by the FBI, The New York Times, The Washington Post, and others. CNN was notably reluctant to cover the story in the run-up to the 2020 election.
4. Covington Catholic / Nick Sandmann confrontation
CNN’s initial coverage strongly portrayed Sandmann and the Covington Catholic students as aggressors toward Native American activist Nathan Phillips. Longer video showed a more complicated scene in which the students were themselves being confronted. CNN settled a defamation lawsuit with Sandmann.
5. Jussie Smollett “MAGA” attack
CNN gave extensive, largely uncritical coverage to Smollett’s claim that he was attacked by two men wearing MAGA hats who shouted racial and homophobic slurs and a pro-Trump slogan. Chicago police later determined it was a staged hoax that Smollett paid two acquaintances to carry out. He was convicted (later overturned on procedural grounds), and the underlying facts of the staging were never seriously disputed.
6. Russian bounties on U.S. troops in Afghanistan
CNN reported as fact (citing anonymous intelligence sources) that Russian military intelligence had offered bounties to Taliban-linked fighters to kill American and British troops. Later assessments by the intelligence community and Biden administration described the intelligence as “low to moderate confidence,” based largely on detainee reporting, and it was not treated as confirmed.
7. “Very fine people” on both sides (Charlottesville)
CNN and its anchors repeatedly stated or implied that Trump had called neo-Nazis and white supremacists “very fine people.” In the same press conference, Trump explicitly said he was not referring to the neo-Nazis and white nationalists, whom he said should be “condemned totally.” He was referring to people on both sides of the statue debate. Snopes rated the common claim False; CNN’s own contemporaneous reporting was more accurate.
8. Operation Tailwind (1998)
CNN and Time ran a major story claiming U.S. special forces used sarin nerve gas against American defectors in Laos in 1970. The network later fully retracted it, concluding there was insufficient evidence. Producers were fired or resigned, and CNN issued a public apology.
9. Joe Rogan taking “horse dewormer”
CNN repeatedly described the ivermectin Rogan took as “horse dewormer.” He had taken the human version prescribed by a doctor. CNN’s own chief medical correspondent, Sanjay Gupta, later acknowledged on Rogan’s podcast that the characterization was misleading.

text:
I’m not quite understanding the pissing-matches of natural disasters.

“OmG HuRriCaNe KaTriNa wAs So mUch WoRse.”

“YoU wOuLdn’t HaVe LaSteD a dAy iN NoRtH CaRoLiNa…”

What did I do when I saw people suffering during Hurricane Helene, in North Carolina? 

I prayed for y’all, and shared your posts.

When the media wasn’t doing y’all justice, thousands of us around the country made sure that’s videos showing what was happening (or NOT happening) was shared to the masses, in hopes it could get you the resources needed.

Did we benefit from every horrific Hurricane before us, like Katrina, Ivan, Opal, or Sally—as they refined, and tightened Hurricane preparedness and responses? Sure did.

Not one person who’s experienced this Hurricane has said their plight is worse than anyone else’s.

Mocking elderly for not being able to use a chainsaw for a 300yr old oak that’s blocking their driveway, 35mi outside of town?  Dipsht vibes.

Laughing at those who didn’t evacuate in NON-evacuation zones, and were unexpectedly pummeled, “Shoulda just left…” is such a weird zinger.

I have to say, the IN-PERSON community I’ve experienced during this disaster has been unmatched, and the silver lining to the storm.

I’ve met neighbors I’ve waved at the last 4yrs, but never had a chance to chat…had a meal with some of them even.

This online ridicule, as people are going through one of their worst nightmares — is despicable.

I saw a post of two veterans, one disabled, who moved here less than two months ago.  They got 2 kids under 3, with another on the way.  Their entire house was ruined by two giant oaks smashing both sides of the house.

I heard an 80yr old woman on the radio, whose husband is in hospice in their home, with a medical bed, and on oxygen.  She didn’t realize she wasn’t strong enough to move the generator to get it set-up (her husband usually did it), and they were left without power, reception, or any means of communication.  Their driveway was blocked by massive trees.  She had to climb through power-line filled limbs, and then a half mile to her neighbors to call the radio station to ask the community for help to clear the tree from her driveway, and help with their generator.

Of course this isn’t geared to everyone who’s suffered a natural disaster — or those who have experienced one of their mentioned ones above — it’s geared to the people who think it’s a flex to marginalize the loss so many people are going through, because apparently loss is a competitive sport.

To the ones who’ve reached out, sent prayers, and offered help — thank you.

To the ones who are mocking people in crisis, y’all need some serious Jesus.

text:
Here are some reasons why visiting Japan 🇯🇵 is a life changing experience:

1) You don’t understand what respect is until you interact with Japanese people. How polite, punctual, kind, helpful, friendly they are. I am from a region in 🇨🇴 where we take pride of our service culture. We’re not even close.

2) That respect is not only towards people. It is also towards their surroundings, maintaining things clean, well kept, following social rules that make life easier for everyone else. One basic example: you see little to no graffiti there.

3) Also, related to #1: I’ve never felt safer in a place than in 🇯🇵 . There might be exceptions, I don’t doubt it, but it feels like you can go anywhere, anytime, and it is OK.

4) Life is everywhere in big cities. The city that never sleeps? Yes, that is probably Tokyo, no doubt. And being the most massive “city” on earth, you feel like night is a completely different trip than the day. Combined with the old school signs, the eating spots, etc it is a vibe like nowhere else.

5) You should get lost in 🇯🇵: and I mean it. Explore, go find some unbeaten path or take a train to a random small fishing town. Those “OG” places are quaint, cozy, perfectly organized. The landmarks are cool? Yes. But it is not why I recommend going there.

6) Some non-western hotel chains are AMAZING. Some of them like Koko or Monday have their hotels in residential areas, and you feel like you are living your life with them. So good.

7) On the not-so-bright side of things, in 🇯🇵 you can understand what a post-growth, post-development society looks like. For about 30 years this country barely grew.

8) (Not an expert here) I think that the combination between stagnant opportunities for a lot of men has created a wide gap between what traditional women expect from men, and what a lot of them can offer. I find these social dynamics fascinating.

9) The result is that if you go to a small town, you’ll probably not see children for hours or even days. Their population is shrinking, we all know that, but their fertility rate within married couples is one of the highest among developed nations. 

10) The problem ends up being that not enough people find partners and marry.
This, to me, should be a lesson on why we need constant growth in our society. 

11) You can grasp the feeling of decadence if you go on a Monday morning to a place where there are big Pachinko places, before opening times. Lines and lines of young men going to spend their time, money and energy at a “not-a-casino”.

12) Enough with the bad stuff. Now my favorite thing about 🇯🇵: how they value craftsmanship. You’ll find restaurants that serve not only amazing Japanese food, but food from anywhere in the world is delicious. Probably the owner has been doing that job for 35 years. And you will see this with ceramics, woodworking, tea ceremonies, knifes, traditional clothing, etc.

13) Talking about craftsmanship, 🇯🇵 is probably the best place in the world to have a hobby. Chances are there is a massive following of whatever you like. From video games, to stationary stores, crafts, music, tech, cars, cooking, knitting, card collecting, anything. It is INSANE and I love it.

14) The seasonal products. 🇯🇵 has a big tradition of companies launching lots of products per year. This is mostly due to seasonality. I read once a book called Nagori, by Japanese author Ryoko Sekiguchi. She does a wonderful job of explaining how important every year’s changes are for their culture. Highly recommend it.

15) Hokkaido milk is no joke. Specially good for soft serve ice creams yum yum 😋.

16) The sounds of 🇯🇵: In this country EVERYTHING talks. The escalators, the stores, the cashier machines at 7-eleven, the trains, the vending machines. I don’t understand anything of what these cute voices say, but I am all for it. Some might find it annoying, though. But not me.

17) The Toyota Alphard Ubers are the most comfortable car in the world.

#japan
